props.title: Layer Cake
props.initialSlug: A drug dealer's last score becomes a deadly maze

sections.content: **Layer Cake** (2004) marked Daniel Craig's breakthrough as a sophisticated London crime boss, essentially serving as his audition for James Bond. Matthew Vaughn's directorial debut brings Guy Ritchie-style British gangster films into a sleeker, more polished era. Unlike the chaotic energy of **Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels** (1998), Layer Cake presents organized crime as a corporate enterprise, where violence happens in elegant settings and criminals wear bespoke suits. The film's unnamed protagonist (Craig) navigates through layers of London's criminal hierarchy while trying to broker one last drug deal before retirement - a classic noir setup elevated by sophisticated direction.

sections.content: Vaughn's direction established a new template for British crime films that influenced works like **Eastern Promises** (2007) and **Legend** (2015). The clinical precision of Layer Cake's violence contrasts sharply with the gleeful chaos of earlier British gangster films. Craig's calculated performance shows organized crime as a business where savvy negotiation matters more than brute force. This shift reflects real changes in London's criminal landscape, where old-school gangsters gave way to sophisticated international networks.

The film's visual style - all cool blues and sterile modernist architecture - influenced a generation of crime thrillers. Compare this to the gritty pub settings of **Get Carter** (1971) or the neon-soaked streets of **Mona Lisa** (1986). Layer Cake's criminal world exists in high-rise offices and upscale restaurants, suggesting that modern crime has more in common with corporate takeovers than street violence. sections.content: Layer Cake bridges classic British gangster films like **The Italian Job** (1969) with modern crime thrillers. Its influence can be seen in works like **Welcome to the Punch** (2013) and **Gangster No. 1** (2000), where criminal enterprises operate like multinational corporations. The film's success also paved the way for Matthew Vaughn's later stylized works like **Kingsman: The Secret Service** (2014), proving that British genre films could compete with Hollywood productions in terms of sophistication and production values.
